decisions.rationale: All 176 comparators were checked. PF-0033 is the same indexing-to-execution non-creation boundary under the Plan-to-Node compilation lifecycle; the other close items are reports, bootstrap permissions, readiness states, activation stages, or consumer-surface authority boundaries.

No comparator governs identity and supersession of repeated PNC-019 certification receipts. Clean-room fixtures, compile-wave receipt identity, and activation outbox delivery have distinct records and lifecycles.

The anchor is the certification-receipt pass/fail recovery state machine. Comparator failures concern readiness disablement, fixture coverage, GUI automation, or runtime-artifact recovery under different authorities.
PF-0052 is a clean-room lifecycle fixture, while the anchor requires receipt fields proving environmental isolation and determinism; their producer, evidence object, and validation lifecycle differ.

No comparator specifies the end-to-end deterministic agent loop. Command operation state, scheduler behavior, and plan-graph ordering are adjacent subsystems with separate authorities and failure contracts.

The anchor owns bridged-provider stream reconnect and breaker replay. The related remote-operation, prompt, tool, async-job, remote-session, and trace retry features have different transports, consumers, and replay identities.

No comparator owns bridged-provider diagnostic identity, optional sequence fallback, and sensitive actor/account references. Tool attribution, UI dispatch correlation, and trace lineage remain distinct schemas.
The anchor is the semantic_failures channel of a certification receipt. Automation status failures, failed-attempt artifacts, and web-job reason metadata have distinct schemas and recovery consumers.
Remote workbench attachment activation is not the same lifecycle as compile restart, remote-session reconnect, executor outbox activation, or runtime-aware compilation.

The anchor concerns capability synchronization readiness. Runtime-disablement readiness, compile readiness, planning degradation, and scheduler blocked state have separate owners and transition triggers.
Command-file project-over-global resolution has a mutation snapshot lifecycle distinct from settings effective-value resolution and subagent required/disabled selection precedence.

The anchor is repository-creation-aware push resumption. Remote reconciliation, generic dispatch cancellation, async jobs, and generic command recovery lack the same SCM authority and external side-effect promise.

Prompt admission owns key/hash collision, client sequence, and execution binding. Dispatch cancellation, prompt replay/rotation, UI dispatch, and generic command recovery occur after or outside admission.

The anchor is the canonical safe-failure promise for stale projections. Orchestrator direct revalidation, route-only surfaces, UI dispatch gating, and widget run-switching are separate consumers and race windows.
Generic GUI stream replay/cursor semantics are distinct from async job resume, remote interactive-session reconnect, and trace retry lineage.

The anchor owns monotonic blocked-event sequence allocation. Blocked outcome classification, prerequisite resume, notice storage, scheduler state, and lineage persistence are separate lifecycle facets.
Provider support-proof freshness and demotion are distinct from widget projection freshness and MCP health/discovery freshness, which have different evidence owners and consumers.

Attempt Recovery is the canonical attempt-state recovery workflow. Concept controls, attempt handoff, retry commands, failed-attempt artifacts, and stored lineage are distinct consumers or persistence lifecycles.
Safe Point Recovery governs recovery execution. Safe-point controls, validity, applicability, planning restore/degradation, and persisted lineage each have distinct authority or lifecycle roles.

The canonical remediation recovery action is narrower than planning restore, lineage propagation, remediation retry-loop control, and the broad remediation-lineage family; those differ in authority and state progression.

PF-0108 represents the same runtime approve/decline/abort decision lifecycle and stale-run race boundary. Graph-scoped HITL, provider pause/resume, configuration snapshotting, and fixed skip/abort command names remain distinct.
Blocked timeout/wait/offline is a canonical state model; outcome semantics, notices, reconnect, handoff records, and scheduler blocked state are separate projections or recovery protocols.

Child Run Ontology is the canonical data model. Policy ceilings, tool child lifecycle, parent-card projection, parallel orchestration, Crew overlay, and lineage artifacts have distinct consumers or lifecycle responsibilities.
Dynamic effective-context shrinking is distinct from run-mode overlay ceilings, descendant authority inheritance, and the user-invoked Compact Now command lifecycle.
The general Runtime Event Catalog has broader authority than UI command events and the goal-only event vocabulary; field conditionality is a separate schema-quality concern.
The canonical runtime event taxonomy and payloads are not the same feature as UI dispatcher events, progress labels, or the goal-specific event schema.

Runtime Surface Readiness concerns live surface availability; compilation disablement, readiness reporting, identifier-only acceptance, and compile-run state are distinct authorities and evidence lifecycles.
Scheduler Blocking Events are event definitions; blocked outcome meaning, resume commands, records, scheduler algorithm, and blocked-state projection have distinct state machines or consumers.
The scheduler Backoff Retry Lifecycle is distinct from remote operation retry, tool deadlines, async jobs, generic command operations, remote sessions, and trace lineage.

PF-0125 restates the same canonical scheduler/recovery invariants and stale-behavior exclusions. Resume-after-prerequisite, wake-cascade mechanics, and blocked-state modeling are separate lifecycle portions.
EP-009 owns blocker-to-canonical-node resolution. Compiler metadata blocking, readiness reports, prerequisite resume, and scheduler blocked state have different authorities and failure inputs.
Executor attempt success/failure transitions are not the same state machine as projected run statuses, progress labels, commands, automation manifests, or web operations.

Replan invalidation governs executor fencing and side-effect reconciliation. Dispatch cancellation, sibling strict-stop, remediation locks, graph publication, and persisted stale lineage each have different authorities or failure contracts.
Canonical executor outcome classification before policy selection is distinct from failover reason preservation, action-field normalization, and remediation-loop control.
Search and SSH owner-classification handoff has no same-feature comparator. Tool attribution and general denial recovery are adjacent but use different classification owners and consumers.
Class-driven executor retry policy is distinct from failover reason continuity, tool deadline budgets, generic command recovery, and remediation retry loops.
Executor's consumer-only classification projection is not page/runtime authority separation, an owner-consumer inventory, or a tool-denial contract.

The anchor asks who selects among executor retry follow-ups. Team decision settings, tool deadline rules, generic commands, and remediation classifiers have different decision authorities and predicates.
Idempotent executor root shutdown is distinct from helper restart, terminal process cleanup, and subagent coordination cleanup.
Executor subprocess grace-window ownership differs from helper-health restart windows, terminal close escalation, and child strict-stop grace.
Graph-integrity prohibition on flattening is distinct from WorkGraph intake staging, graph-generation publication, and plan-graph execution ordering.
PF-0143 covers the same runtime scheduler ready-set ordering and fairness lifecycle, including missing claim and ordering rules. Plan-graph execution ordering is a distinct compile/graph authority.

PF-0055 includes the same blocked-versus-failed collision and precedence semantics under the runtime outcome lifecycle. Projected status aggregation, approval races, and scheduler blocked behavior are distinct.

PF-0143 is the same runtime scheduler capacity, ready-set claim, and deferred-work lifecycle. Concept inputs, compile parallel stages, global ceilings, discovery scheduling, and child orchestration have separate owners.

The graph-integrity fail-stop owns executor treatment of in-flight mutation attempts. Dispatch cancellation, child strict-stop, graph publication, and plan ordering have different triggers and cleanup obligations.
Canonical execution_unit_context scope is distinct from prompt handoff, mode overlays, chat actor identity, and execution-policy disclosure.
Tier-era context retirement is a compatibility rule, not retired feature coverage, runtime-mode canon, mode normalization, or descendant overlay narrowing.
Attempt counter allocation and attempt-record dispatch atomicity differ from kill counters, denial exclusions, failed-attempt artifact content, and lineage persistence.
The executor replan_generation counter's overflow and atomic application are distinct from kill counters, orchestrator graph publication authority, and persisted stale-generation lineage.

Thread binding and mode-transition atomicity has no same-feature comparator. Revalidation, debug resume, projection gating, focused-run switching, and identity disclosure have distinct binding subjects.
Executor mutation preflight freshness is related to several validation-to-action races, but each comparator governs a different surface, target identity, or dispatch lifecycle.
Executor fallback attempt-limit precedence differs from concept concurrency inputs, global run ceilings, tool retry deadlines, and subagent parallel-cap ownership.
Attempt-counter mismatch recovery selection has a distinct authority and predicate from kill counters, remediation loops, broad remediation lineage, and stored attempt lineage.
Generic detached-panel identity is distinct from terminal live-state ownership, terminal attachment continuity, the terminal process lifecycle, and developer-panel commands.
Remote terminal presentation security has a distinct trust boundary from container URLs, SCM lineage, usage payloads, chat commands, and developer-panel evidence.
The runtime workgroup information architecture is not the Node Graph concept surface, developer runtime panels, or chat goal evidence display; each serves different consumers and promises.
Editor embedding is a GUI consumer promise; terminal live-state ownership, attachment recovery, and pane/process lifecycle are authoritative runtime features with distinct actions and failure states.
Terminal drag-and-drop transactionality is a dock/layout transfer operation, not shell/edit races, a generic command lifecycle, or terminal process cleanup.
Reduced-motion dock behavior has no same-feature comparator. Help accessibility, progress presentation, and developer panels have separate consumer promises and no shared motion lifecycle.
The generic panel dock state machine differs from progress states, terminal pane/process state, and developer runtime panel controls.
GUI undock triggers are distinct from terminal live-state ownership, terminal continuity, and the terminal detach/process lifecycle, which govern runtime effects after a surface action.

All 176 comparators were exhaustively checked; none governs snap-zone geometry overlap and precedence under the detachable-panel layout authority. Shared GUI or state-machine vocabulary was insufficient.
